title: Piotroski uses `!= null` (not isFinite) for balance fields, so a NaN balance value adds a phantom always-failing signal that corrupts both the F-score and the scaled threshold (0.15-weight TURNAROUND input)
evidence: `_balanceVal` (lines 33-37) returns `arr[idx] && arr[idx][field]` (raw, no finite guard). Signal guards use `!= null`, e.g. line 93: `if (debt0 != null && debt1 != null && ...)`. Since `NaN != null` is true, a NaN debt0 enters the signal: `lev0 = debt0/assets0 = NaN`, then line 96 `pass: lev0 < lev1` -> `NaN < x` -> false. Reproduced with `totalDebt:NaN`: delta_leverage AND delta_liquidity both INCLUDED and scored 0; F-score 5/8 instead of 5/6 (the two NaN signals should have been excluded), threshold still scaled against 8.
why_it_matters: Two effects compound: (1) phantom signals are counted as failed (depressing score), and (2) `signals.length` is inflated, so `scaledThreshold = round(6*length/8)` (line 130) demands more passes than the data supports — a stock with genuinely 6 computable signals can be judged against an 8-signal denominator. piotroski-f-score is 0.15 weight in TURNAROUND. NaN balance fields are plausible from partial Yahoo parses (pull-yahoo trims trailing nulls but mid-array bad values survive).
fix: Make `_balanceVal` finite-guarded (`Number.isFinite(v) ? v : null`) exactly like beneish/ohlson, and/or change every signal guard from `x != null` to `Number.isFinite(x)`. This both excludes non-finite inputs from `signals.length` and prevents the NaN-comparison-false trap. Comment: 'prevents failure mode: NaN balance field added as phantom failed signal, corrupting score and scaled threshold'.

_verdict.note: CONFIRMED by reproduction in C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/methods/piotroski-f-score.js. _balanceVal (lines 33-37) returns `arr[idx] && arr[idx][field]` with NO finite guard, unlike the sibling forensic methods beneish-m-score.js (line 97: `return Number.isFinite(v) ? v : null;`) and ohlson-o-score.js (line 98: same). The signal guards use `!= null` (e.g. line 93 delta_leverage, line 100 delta_liquidity), and since `NaN != null` is true, a NaN balance field enters the signal. Reproduced exactly as claimed with totalDebt:NaN at idx 0: both delta_leverage and delta_liquidity were INCLUDED and scored 0 (NaN<x and NaN>x both false), giving F-score 5/8 with maxPossible:8 / scaledThreshold:6 / pass:false. The correct missing-data path (totalDebt absent rather than NaN) excludes both signals, giving 5/6 / scaledThreshold:5 / pass:true. So one phantom NaN field flips the verdict from PASS to FAIL — it corrupts both the numerator (extra always-failing signals) and the scaled-threshold denominator (signals.length stays 8 instead of 6). Severity high is justified: piotroski feeds the 0.15-weight TURNAROUND composite input, and NaN propagation from upstream parsing is exactly the failure mode the sibling methods already defend against.

title: Metric-divergence-guard is structurally blind on 'computed-margin' snapshots (annual margin is tautologically equal to TTM margin)
evidence: Guard: `const ttmMargin = H.metricValue(stock,'operatingMargin'); ... const annualMargin = oi0/rev0*100; const divergence = Math.abs(ttmMargin-annualMargin);` (lines 57,71-72). But pull-yahoo.js _deriveOpIncForFinancials() path 3 sets `annualOpInc[y] = annualRev[y] * operatingMargins_TTM` (pull-yahoo.js:589-596) and stamps `meta.opIncSource='computed-margin'` (pull-yahoo.js:848). For any such snapshot oi0/rev0 == operatingMargins_TTM, so annualMargin == ttmMargin and divergence == 0 ALWAYS. metricValue returns pp (pull-yahoo.js:895 multiplies by 100; header line 14 confirms 'pp'), oi0/rev0*100 is also pp — units match, so the cancellation is exact. The method never reads meta.opIncSource.
why_it_matters: This guard's whole purpose (header lines 4-9) is to catch financial/treasury entities like MSTR where TTM diverges from annual op income. Those are exactly the snapshots most likely to hit the Financial-Services-gated 'computed-margin' fallback, where annualOpInc is synthesized FROM the TTM margin — so the very names the guard targets get a guaranteed divergence of 0 and silently PASS. It is a DATAGUARD (method-types.js:74), so a false pass lets a data-anomalous stock into picks.
fix: Read `stock.meta.opIncSource`; when it is 'computed-margin' the annual-vs-TTM comparison is non-independent — return computable:false with reason 'annualOpInc derived from TTM margin (opIncSource=computed-margin) — divergence undefined'. Add comment: 'prevents tautological pass when annual op-income was back-derived from the TTM operating margin'.

_verdict.note: CONFIRMED real with full source evidence. Tautology chain verified: (1) guard computes annualMargin = oi0/rev0*100 (metric-divergence-guard.js:71) and ttmMargin = H.metricValue(stock,'operatingMargin') (line 57); (2) metricValue returns metrics.operatingMargin.value which is set to _y(fd,'operatingMargins')*100 in pp (pull-yahoo.js:895, _helpers.js metricValue:23-29); (3) for opIncSource=='computed-margin' snapshots, annualOpInc[y]=annualRev[y]*operatingMargins (pull-yahoo.js:589-596, and the post-FTS retry at 1973-1976 which uses _opMargFrac = operatingMargin.value/100 = same operatingMargins fraction). So annualMargin = (rev*operatingMargins)/rev*100 = operatingMargins*100 = ttmMargin EXACTLY -> divergence==0 -> always passes the <=1000pp gate. Units are both pp so cancellation is exact; FX conversion (pull-yahoo.js:1985) multiplies oi and rev by the same rate and cancels in the ratio, so it does not break the tautology. grep confirms NO method in methods/ reads meta.opIncSource — the guard (and siblings) are blind to the provenance flag that pull-yahoo.js:848/1976 deliberately stamps; the code's own comment (pull-yahoo.js:520-523) acknowledges path 3 'folds year-by-year volatility into a single TTM margin. Methods can flag this as derived via meta.opIncSource' — i.e. the hazard is documented but never wired up. NUANCE on the 'ALWAYS' wording: computed-margin is sector-gated (pull-yahoo.js:639, 1971-1972) — fires only for Financial Services tickers whose Yahoo native operatingIncome is null and the bank/insurance line-item paths failed. Within that subset the guard is structurally blind and rubber-stamps every value (pass, divergence=0). This is a real false-negative in a data-integrity DataGuard exactly for the anomaly class it exists to catch, so high is warranted. fix_safe=true: reading stock.meta.opIncSource and returning computable:false for 'computed-margin' is behavior-preserving for all other snapshots, only converts the meaningless tautological pass into computable:false, and matches the existing computable:false / H.buildResult pattern already used at lines 52 and 64. Low risk to auto-apply.

title: Quarterly net-income FTS extraction uses raw r.netIncome — misses NetIncome / netIncomeContinuousOperations casing, unlike the annual path
evidence: ftsQuarterlyNI = (fts.quarterlyFin || []).slice().reverse().map(r => r && r.netIncome != null ? r.netIncome : null);  // vs annual path line 1102: const ni = _ftsValue(r, 'netIncome', 'NetIncome', 'netIncomeContinuousOperations');
why_it_matters: Yahoo FTS rows for many tickers emit PascalCase ('NetIncome') or the GAAP-continuous variant ('netIncomeContinuousOperations') instead of camelCase 'netIncome' (the file itself documents this drift at lines 1054-1064 and 1099-1102). That silently disables the 8-quarter earnings-stability method (Tag-90) — exactly the kind of method that should separate the screener's '20% of potential' from its full power. The bug is masked because nulls look like 'Yahoo didn't provide it' rather than 'we read the wrong key'.
fix: Route through the existing helper: `.map(r => { const v = (r != null) ? _ftsValue(r, 'netIncome', 'NetIncome', 'netIncomeContinuousOperations') : null; return v != null ? v : null; });`. No FTS_CACHE_VERSION bump needed (read-shape change only; affects freshly-parsed rows). Comment the failure mode: 'prevents all-null quarterly-NI when Yahoo FTS emits PascalCase/continuous-ops netIncome key'.

_verdict.note: Confirmed real inconsistency. pull-yahoo.js:1836-1837 extracts quarterly NI with raw `r.netIncome` only (single camelCase key, no fallback), while the annual path at line 1102 uses `_ftsValue(r, 'netIncome', 'NetIncome', 'netIncomeContinuousOperations')`. Both consume the SAME raw FTS rows: `fts.quarterlyFin` is also fed to mapFTSToQuarterly (line 1810), which at lines 1216-1220 uses `_ftsValue(r, 'totalRevenue', 'TotalRevenue')` etc. — proving the codebase itself treats quarterly FTS rows as PascalCase-prone. So the quarterly NI path uniquely fails to handle PascalCase/continuous-ops casing AND skips the snake_case fallback `_ftsValue` provides (line 1062). Downstream impact: canonical.timeseries.netIncomeQ (line 1931) → quarterly-earnings-stability.js and earnings-surprise-momentum, plus the data-quality gate `timeseries.netIncomeQ>=4` (data-quality.js:73). Severity downgraded to medium: this only bites when Yahoo emits the non-camelCase key for quarterly rows (an edge case, not the dominant path — camelCase `netIncome` is the normal emission, same as `totalRevenue` being the primary tried key). When it does bite, it degrades gracefully to all-null (no corruption, no positional misalignment), costing only a 0.5-weight data-quality point and disabling two quarterly methods for that ticker.

title: EV/EBITDA accepts Yahoo's enterpriseToEbitda whenever it is >0, silently ignoring negative-EBITDA firms that Yahoo encodes as a negative ratio
evidence: Line 27: `if (yahooRatio != null && yahooRatio > 0) { ... pass: yahooRatio <= THRESHOLD ... }`. When a firm has negative EBITDA, Yahoo's enterpriseToEbitda comes back NEGATIVE (EV>0 / EBITDA<0). The `> 0` filter drops straight through to the manual fallback — but the fallback's own EBITDA guard is `opInc*1.2` and `if (ebitda <= 0) return computable:false`. So negative-EBITDA names end up non-computable, which is correct ONLY by luck of the fallback. The real defect: a firm with a tiny POSITIVE EBITDA and huge EV yields a Yahoo ratio like 850 — that is correctly failed. But a firm whose Yahoo ratio is a small negative number (e.g. -2, near-zero negative EBITDA) is treated as 'use fallback', and if the fallback's opInc happens to be positive it can PASS at a low EV/EBITDA while the company is actually unprofitable on an EBITDA basis.
why_it_matters: EV/EBITDA is a `lte` valuation gate; the whole point is to reject expensive names. A near-breakeven company can flip between 'Yahoo negative ratio → ignored' and 'fallback opInc*1.2 positive → cheap PASS', producing a valuation verdict that contradicts the native ratio. The branch silently prefers the heuristic over Yahoo's own (more accurate) number for exactly the marginal-profitability names where the answer matters most.
fix: Treat a non-null Yahoo ratio as authoritative regardless of sign: when `yahooRatio != null` and `yahooRatio <= 0`, return computable:false with reason 'negative/zero EBITDA per Yahoo native ratio — EV/EBITDA not meaningful' instead of falling through to the heuristic. Only fall back when `yahooRatio == null`. Add comment naming the failure mode: 'prevents heuristic opInc*1.2 PASS overriding Yahoo's negative-EBITDA signal'.

_verdict.note: Confirmed against source. methods/ev-ebitda.js:27 is exactly `if (yahooRatio != null && yahooRatio > 0)`, so a NEGATIVE Yahoo enterpriseToEbitda falls through to the manual fallback. pull-yahoo.js:910 passes Yahoo's `enterpriseToEbitda` through raw (`_metric(_y(ks,'enterpriseToEbitda'),...)`) with no sign filtering, so a negative ratio (EV>0 / negative TTM-EBITDA) is real input. The key point: the fallback uses a DIFFERENT metric and period than Yahoo's ratio — `opInc = latestAnnual('annualOpInc')` (most recent full fiscal-year operating income, pull-yahoo.js:1100/1106), while Yahoo's ratio uses TTM EBITDA from financialData. So a name that has slipped to negative TTM EBITDA but still had a positive last-FY operating income passes the fallback's `ebitda = opInc*1.2 > 0` guard (line 67) and can emit a PASS at a low EV/EBITDA. The auditor's evidence is self-contradictory in spots (it concedes the clean co-negative case IS caught by the fallback "by luck") — but the divergence case is genuine and not caught. Downstream this matters: generate-methods-report.js:246 only excludes a stock when `computable===true && pass===false`; a false PASS keeps the stock with a valuation endorsement, whereas computable:false would be neutral. So the bug turns a should-be-neutral, EBITDA-negative name into a passing valuation gate. NOT high though — it is a narrow TTM-vs-annual divergence window on one of many gates, neutral-vs-pass (not a hard wrong-exclusion or broad silent corruption); revised to medium. The proposed fix (treat non-null yahooRatio <= 0 as computable:false) is consistent with the file's own existing `ev <= 0` (line 59) and `ebitda <= 0` (line 67) non-computable guards and with the Tag 219 "Yahoo native ratio is authoritative" design intent.

title: Vacuous-pass: five 'fail-case' tests assert only !r.pass without guarding r.computable
evidence: ROIC fail (64-68): `const r = ...['roic']; if (r.pass) throw new Error('should fail (10% < 15%)');` — no `r.computable` check, no value check. Same shape at Net-Debt/EBITDA fail (84-88: `if (r.pass) throw new Error('should fail');`), Revenue-Growth-3Y fail (121-125), FCF-Yield fail (133-137), GM-Stability fail (149-156). Contrast the Rule-of-40 fail case (43-48) which is safe because line 47 also asserts `approx(r.value, 25)`, and every PASS-case which asserts `r.computable`.
why_it_matters: A result with computable:false carries pass:false (verified across the suite's contract). If a refactor accidentally makes any of these methods return incomputable for valid input (a missing-field guard regressing, an envelope-unwrap break, a thrown error swallowed to a default), the method is silently broken but these tests stay GREEN — they cannot distinguish 'correctly failed the gate' from 'never evaluated'. This is exactly the silent-method-drop failure class the suite elsewhere (line 160) tries to defend against.
fix: Add `if (!r.computable) throw new Error('should be computable')` before the `if (r.pass)` line in each of the five fail-case tests, OR add a positive value assertion (e.g. ROIC fail should also assert `approx(r.value, 0.10)`). Cheapest: insert the computable guard. This pins the fail-case to a real computed FAIL, not a vacuous incomputable.

_verdict.note:
Confirmed the structural weakness, but the "vacuous-pass" label overstates it. buildResult() in methods/_helpers.js (lines 58-68) forces pass:!!pass, and wrapEvaluate (lines 310-319) turns any thrown error into computable:false with pass:false — so a test that only asserts `if (r.pass) throw` does NOT fire when a method regresses to incomputable. That is a genuine missing-guard gap in all five cited fail-cases (tag28-tests.js: ROIC 64-68, Net-Debt/EBITDA 84-88, Revenue-Growth-3Y 121-125, FCF-Yield 133-137, GM-Stability 149-156). The contrast is also accurate: Rule-of-40 fail (line 47) additionally asserts approx(r.value,25), so it is regression-safe; every PASS-case asserts r.computable.

HOWEVER, none of the five tests is actually vacuous TODAY. I traced each input through its method and all five currently produce computable:true, pass:false (genuine computed FAILs): ROIC value=0.10 (10/100); Net-Debt/EBITDA value=50/12=4.17 (EBITDA=opInc*1.2=12); Rev-Growth-3Y CAGR≈9.1% (130 vs 100); FCF-Yield 0.02 (2e9/100e9, floored threshold 0.05); GM-Stability CoV≈0.29 (mean .45/sample-std .129). So the tests pass for the right reason now; the risk is a FUTURE silent regression to incomputable going uncaught — exactly the silent-method-drop class the suite guards elsewhere (line 160 test). That makes this a legitimate test-hardening item, but it is a latent test-robustness gap with zero current production or test-pass impact — medium, not high.

Fix is safe to auto-apply: inserting `if (!r.computable) throw new Error('should be computable')` before each `if (r.pass)` line is behavior-preserving (all five inputs compute today, so the new assertion passes immediately) and matches the existing idiom used throughout the file.

title: parseFloat(...) || DEFAULT pattern for treasury yield and pass threshold: a legitimate env value of '0' silently falls back to the default (falsy-zero bug)
evidence: `const treasuryYield = parseFloat(process.env.BUFFETT_TREASURY_YIELD_10Y) || TREASURY_YIELD_DEFAULT;` (line 423) and `const threshold = parseFloat(process.env.BUFFETT_PASS_THRESHOLD) || PASS_THRESHOLD_DEFAULT;` (line 755). If an operator sets BUFFETT_TREASURY_YIELD_10Y=0 (zero-rate scenario / test) or BUFFETT_PASS_THRESHOLD=0 (accept-all), parseFloat returns 0 which is falsy, so the default (0.045 / 0.85) is used instead.
why_it_matters: This is the '|| 0'-class falsy bug inverted: 0 is a legitimately valid configured value that gets discarded. For the threshold, an intended 0 (diagnostic / let-everything-through run) silently becomes 0.85. NaN from a malformed env string also falls back (acceptable) but masks misconfiguration without warning.
fix: Parse then explicitly check Number.isFinite: `const t = parseFloat(env); treasuryYield = Number.isFinite(t) ? t : DEFAULT;`. Add comment: `// prevents env value 0 from being discarded by falsy || default`.

_verdict.note: Confirmed against source in C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/methods/buffett-criteria.js. Both cited lines match exactly: line 423 `const treasuryYield = parseFloat(process.env.BUFFETT_TREASURY_YIELD_10Y) || TREASURY_YIELD_DEFAULT;` and line 755 `const threshold = parseFloat(process.env.BUFFETT_PASS_THRESHOLD) || PASS_THRESHOLD_DEFAULT;`. Defaults are nonzero (line 35 PASS_THRESHOLD_DEFAULT=0.85, line 36 TREASURY_YIELD_DEFAULT=0.045), so a legitimate env value of exactly '0' yields parseFloat('0')===0 (falsy) and is silently discarded in favor of the default — a genuine falsy-zero bug. Behavioral impact verified: treasuryYield feeds the T8 earnings-yield-vs-Treasury comparison (line 447 `pass = pretaxEY > treasuryYield`), and threshold gates the overall pass at line 760 (`passRate >= threshold`). Setting BUFFETT_PASS_THRESHOLD=0 (intended accept-all) would silently re-impose the 85% gate; BUFFETT_TREASURY_YIELD_10Y=0 (zero-rate test) would silently use 4.5%. These are the only two references to these env vars in the worktree (grep-confirmed), so no other parse layer mitigates it. Real but edge-triggered: it only manifests when an operator explicitly sets the var to 0; normal unset/valid use is unaffected. Severity medium is reasonable (accept-all=0 misconfig is a plausible operator footgun, no silent corruption in default operation).

title: Non-atomic fs.writeFileSync into fundamentals-cache bypasses the repo's writeFileAtomic — SIGKILL/CI-timeout mid-write truncates a court-screen input file
evidence: Line 175 `const j = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(cacheFile, 'utf8'));` then line 180 `fs.writeFileSync(cacheFile, JSON.stringify(j));`. This is a read-modify-write on a committed-state file with a plain writeFileSync. The other three scripts in this batch all import and use `const { writeFileAtomic } = require('../lib/atomic-write.js')` precisely because (per lib/atomic-write.js header) plain writeFileSync left ≥9 state files truncatable: 'A SIGKILL / CI timeout mid-write truncated the file; downstream ... then aborted on parse-error or worse, silently loaded a {} shape and regenerated everything from scratch'. enrich-q-revenue.js does NOT import atomic-write at all.
why_it_matters: fundamentals-cache/{TICKER}.json is consumed by court-screen.js (durability v3, confirmed: grep revQYoYsec → court-screen.js). A crash between the open-for-write truncation and full flush leaves the WHOLE fundamentals payload (not just revQYoYsec) as a half-written/zero-byte file. The next court-screen run then JSON.parse-throws or silently loses every fundamental for that ticker. Worse than the form4 scripts because here the truncation destroys pre-existing data the script only meant to augment.
fix: Import writeFileAtomic from ../lib/atomic-write.js (same one-line require the sibling scripts use) and replace `fs.writeFileSync(cacheFile, JSON.stringify(j))` with `writeFileAtomic(cacheFile, JSON.stringify(j))`. No FTS_CACHE_VERSION touched; this is a scripts/ file, not methods/index.js.

_verdict.note: Confirmed at scripts/enrich-q-revenue.js:175-180: a read-modify-write (read line 175, mutate j.payload.ftsQuarterly lines 177-179, write line 180) uses plain fs.writeFileSync(cacheFile, JSON.stringify(j)), and the script never imports lib/atomic-write.js. The sibling-convention claim holds: ~25 scripts under scripts/ import { writeFileAtomic } from ../lib/atomic-write.js, and the lib header (lines 2-23) documents exactly the SIGKILL/CI-timeout mid-write truncation hazard. The downstream-consumer claim also holds: court-screen.js:134 reads payload.ftsQuarterly.revQYoYsec to compute the durability metric, so a truncated/empty file would silently degrade that input. So the defect is genuine and matches a real, repo-recognized pattern. BUT the finding's framing overstates the blast radius: it calls the target a 'committed-state file', whereas fundamentals-cache/ is gitignored (.gitignore:16-18 — '28-day local cache; not needed in git history, rebuilt on each runner'). The file is a rebuildable local cache, not committed state; the script is deterministic and idempotent (re-run rebuilds from SEC companyfacts.zip), and the cache regenerates on each runner. A mid-write truncation is recoverable by re-running, unlike the truly-committed state files atomic-write was built for. That justifies downgrading high -> medium.

title: txnKey omits price/owner → two real same-day same-share buys at different prices (multi-lot) collapse to one; identical key in backfill-form345 means the bug is repo-wide

title: Filing-lag gate (gate4) has no lower bound — a filingDate before the transactionDate passes via negative lag
evidence: `const lagDays = (filingMs - mostRecentBuy.tMs) / DAY_MS; gate4 = lagDays <= MAX_FILING_LAG_DAYS;` There is an upper bound (<=90d) but no `lagDays >= 0` check. A corrupt or mis-parsed filingDate earlier than transactionDate yields a negative lagDays, which satisfies `<= 90` and passes the gate.

Low severity because it requires bad cache data, but the gate exists precisely to validate data sanity.

Failure mode is permissive (a garbage record clears the gate) rather than a crash, and the other three gates (buys exist, min buy value, net positive) still apply, so blast radius is small. Low severity is appropriate.

title: jaccard() doc-comment says 'Jaccard distance' but the function returns Jaccard SIMILARITY (intersection/union)
evidence: Line 41 comment: 'Jaccard distance = |A ∩ B| / |A ∪ B|. 1.0 = identical, 0.0 = no overlap.' That formula and the 1.0=identical semantics are the Jaccard *index/similarity*; Jaccard *distance* = 1 - that. The code (line 48 `inter / union`) correctly computes similarity, matching how it is consumed (line 172 `m.jaccard >= 0.7 ? 'jac-good'`), so behavior is fine — only the term 'distance' is wrong.
why_it_matters: Mislabeled metric in an audit doc invites a future 'fix' that inverts it (1 - x) to match the word 'distance', which would silently flip every stability threshold (0.7 good becomes 0.3 good). Terminology bugs in shared diagnostics are how downstream regressions get introduced.
fix: Change the comment to 'Jaccard similarity (index)' and keep the formula/behavior.

_verdict.note: Confirmed by source. scripts/pick-diff.js line 41 comment reads "Jaccard distance = |A ∩ B| / |A ∪ B|. 1.0 = identical, 0.0 = no overlap." The formula intersection/union and the "1.0=identical" semantics are the Jaccard similarity/index, NOT distance (distance = 1 - similarity, where 1.0 would mean no overlap). title: isInvalidSymbol length>12 heuristic can false-positive-prune legitimate long symbols
evidence: `if (ticker.length > 12 && !/[.\-:^]/.test(ticker)) return 'looks-like-company-name';` (line 65). The rationale targets literal company-name entries like 'STMicroelectronics' (15 chars). But the rule prunes ANY separator-free symbol over 12 chars, with no requirement that it be alphabetic — and prune is destructive (rewrites watchlist.json via writeFileAtomic).
why_it_matters: Some legitimate Yahoo symbols (certain mutual-fund classes, structured products, and crypto pairs) exceed 12 chars without dot/dash/caret. Such an entry would be silently evicted as 'looks-like-company-name' and, once removed from the committed watchlist, only recoverable from git history. Currently 0 live entries trip it, so it's latent — but it's a hardcoded-shape heuristic doing irreversible deletion.
fix: Tighten the guard so it only matches the actual failure mode: require it to be all-alpha AND mixed-case (real symbols are upper-case), e.g. `ticker.length > 12 && /[a-z]/.test(ticker) && !/[.\-:^ ]/.test(ticker)`. This still catches 'STMicroelectronics' but spares all-caps long symbols. Comment the precise failure mode it prevents.

_verdict.note:
Confirmed real (low severity), with the caveat that no current data triggers it. Code at C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/scripts/prune-watchlist.js:65 reads `if (ticker.length > 12 && !/[.\-:^]/.test(ticker)) return 'looks-like-company-name';`. The guard is genuinely broader than its stated intent (catching literal company-name entries like 'STMicroelectronics'): it matches ANY separator-free string >12 chars with no alpha/case requirement, so a hypothetical long all-caps or all-digit symbol would be silently dropped. The $-preferred-share case is already handled separately at line 62, so this length rule is purely the company-name backstop.

Practical likelihood is very low, which justifies 'low' severity. I scanned the live watchlist.json (23,748 entries): ZERO entries are flagged by this heuristic. Longest no-separator ticker is 'YASKAWA' (7 chars); no-separator length histogram tops out at 7 with only 3 entries >5 chars. All long real symbols (ESSITY-B.ST, MAERSK-B.CO, 005930.KS) contain '.'/'-' and are exempt. So the false-positive is currently latent, not active.

fix_safe=true: the proposed change adds `/[a-z]/.test(ticker)` (require mixed-case) plus a space in the negated class. This strictly NARROWS a destructive operation (fewer deletions), still catches the one documented target 'STMicroelectronics' (has lowercase), and is behavior-identical on all current data (0 entries affected either way) — it only diverges in the safer direction on hypothetical edge cases. Low risk to auto-apply.

title: getMcap lacks the Number.isFinite guard that strategy-modes uses — NaN marketCap propagates into pick output
evidence: function getMcap(stock){ const m = stock.marketCap || (stock.meta && stock.meta.marketCap); if (typeof m === 'number') return m; if (m && typeof m === 'object' && 'value' in m) return m.value; return null; }  — contrast methods/strategy-modes.js line 192-194 which does `if (mcUnwrapped == null || !Number.isFinite(mcUnwrapped)) return mcap_missing`.
why_it_matters: If marketCap.value is NaN or Infinity, getMcap returns it verbatim into the pick. JSON.stringify(NaN) serializes as null so the on-disk vintage is not corrupted, but the value flows through in-memory consumers and the asymmetry with strategy-modes (which treats NaN mcap as 'missing') means the same stock can be mcap_missing for gating yet carry a non-null in-memory mcap here. Minor NaN-propagation / no-isFinite-guard instance the audit asks for.
fix: Mirror strategy-modes: `const v = (typeof m === 'number') ? m : (m && typeof m === 'object' && 'value' in m ? m.value : null); return Number.isFinite(v) ? v : null;`

_verdict.note:
Verified the behavioral difference is real. snapshot-picks.js:61-66 getMcap unwraps {value} and returns it with no finiteness check, while methods/strategy-modes.js:191-194 guards `if (mcUnwrapped == null || !Number.isFinite(mcUnwrapped))`. So a NaN marketCap.value would be returned by getMcap unguarded. The title's claim of a real inconsistency is accurate.

HOWEVER the impact is overstated and the severity is correctly LOW (arguably borderline cosmetic):
- getMcap has exactly ONE caller (snapshot-picks.js:105) and its return value goes only into the `marketCap` OUTPUT field of a pick. It is NOT used for sorting (picks.sort uses score/primaryMetric.value, lines 250-260), filtering, the mcap floor, or any selection logic. So a NaN cannot change which stocks are picked or their order.
- The pick object is written via JSON.stringify (lines 283/285). JSON.stringify(NaN) === "null", so even an unguarded NaN serializes to `"marketCap": null` in the output file — identical to what the proposed fix emits explicitly. The observable JSON is the same with or without the guard.
- NaN reaching the snapshot at all is a narrow edge case: pull-yahoo.js wraps marketCap via _metric() and applies a floor filter (lines 2007-2018) that skips null/out-of-range mcap. NaN would slip past the floor (NaN comparisons are false, and NaN != null) only in the rare event Yahoo returns NaN or the price-only path computes q.marketCap*tradingFactor === NaN.

Net: genuine defensive-consistency gap worth closing to match the sibling function, but no functional corruption of picks and no different output bytes in practice. LOW is right.
